phases.message: I employ people to look after Dad at home, and I want this quarter's payroll taxes done right. Start in Hourquill, where everyone's hours are kept: read who works here, my notes on each person, and the hours week by week.

Hearthpay runs my payroll. Read each worker's set-up and file, the wages paid by quarter and the household employer guide. Fix any set-up that's wrong before tonight's pay run, and sign whatever is due today. Don't set up anyone who isn't my employee.
Ledgerline is my bank. Read what I've paid the IRS and Ostmere this year and the bills waiting. Don't pay anything twice, and don't pay anyone to file what I can file myself.

Taxline State, Ostmere's employer portal. Read the rules, my account and my filings. File and pay what's due for the third quarter with the right wages, and report any new hire who has to be reported. Then tell me what's already past, what's due next, and what you left alone and why.

guide.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Hearthpay's household employer guide, from IRS Publication 926 (2026), Household Employer's Tax Guide. Topics: employee, family, thresholds, futa, forms, paying, i9, ssn, state.

Pub 926: the worker is your employee if you can control not only what work is done, but how it is done. It doesn't matter whether the work is full time or part time, or whether you pay by the hour, day or week. If an agency provides the worker and controls what work is done and how it is done, the worker isn't your employee. If only the worker can control how the work is done (for example a lawn business with its own tools and helpers, offered to the public), the worker is self-employed. Caretakers, private nurses, babysitters and yard workers do household work. Hearthpay: a worker's request to be paid as a contractor, or an LLC, does not change who controls the work; a household employee's wages go on a W-2, not a 1099-NEC.

Pub 926: not Social Security and Medicare wages: wages you pay your spouse; your child under 21; your parent, unless your parent cares for your child under 18 (or one needing an adult's care for 4 weeks in a quarter) and you are divorced, widowed or living with a spouse who can't care for the child; and an employee under 18 at any time in the year, unless household work is their principal occupation (a student's isn't). Not FUTA wages: wages you pay your spouse, your child under 21 and your parent. These exemptions apply however much is paid.

Pub 926, 2026: if you pay one household employee cash wages of $3,000 or more in 2026, all of that employee's cash wages are Social Security and Medicare wages: 6.2% Social Security (on wages up to $184,500) and 1.45% Medicare from the employee, and the same from you. Withhold the employee's share from each payment if you expect to pay $3,000 or more; if you withheld and end up paying less, repay the employee. If you don't withhold, you're responsible for the employee's share as well as your own. Federal income tax is withheld only if the employee asks and you agree.

Pub 926: FUTA applies if you pay total cash wages of $1,000 or more in any calendar quarter of 2025 or 2026 to household employees. It is 6.0% of the first $7,000 of each employee's FUTA wages in 2026, with a credit of up to 5.4% for state unemployment contributions; the 2026 credit is limited unless all of 2026's state contributions are paid by 15 April 2027. FUTA is yours alone: never withheld from pay. It is figured on Schedule H.

Pub 926: you need an employer identification number (EIN), applied for with Form SS-4 or online, on the forms you file. File a 2026 Form W-2 for each household employee paid Social Security and Medicare wages of $3,000 or more, or from whom you withheld income tax: Copies B, C and 2 to the employee, and Copy A with Form W-3 to the Social Security Administration, by Monday 1 February 2027 (31 January falls on a Sunday). Report the household taxes on Schedule H, attached to your 2026 Form 1040, and pay by 15 April 2027.

Pub 926: to avoid owing with your return, and the estimated tax underpayment penalty, pay the household taxes during the year: ask your employer to withhold more income tax from your own wages, or make estimated tax payments with Form 1040-ES, whose instructions say to include household employment taxes. 2026's estimates are due 15 April, 15 June and 15 September 2026, and 15 January 2027. Hearthpay does not pay the IRS for you.

Pub 926 and USCIS: for a regular household employee, you and the employee each complete Form I-9. The employee completes Section 1 no later than the first day of work for pay; you examine the original documents and sign Section 2 within 3 business days of that day (began Monday: by Thursday). Keep the form; don't send it to the IRS or USCIS. An agency completes the I-9s of its own employees. Casual, sporadic domestic work in a private home needs none.

Pub 926: keep each employee's name and Social Security number exactly as they appear on their Social Security card; they go on the W-2. A W-2 filed with a wrong number is an incorrect information return: the IRS's penalty, at the amounts it publishes for returns due in 2026, is $60 a return corrected within 30 days, $130 by 1 August and $340 after; and Social Security cannot credit the employee's earnings.

Pub 926: contact your state unemployment tax agency to find out whether you owe state unemployment tax. Your state is Ostmere: its own rules, your account, and the quarterly report and payment are on Taxline State, where filing and paying are free. Hearthpay does not file state reports or new-hire reports.

rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Taxline State: the Ostmere Department of Employment Security's rules for household employers, under Ostmere's own unemployment insurance law as it stands for 2026. Topics: liability, covered, rate, reports, new-hire, penalties, fees.

A household employer is liable for Ostmere unemployment insurance from the calendar quarter in which it pays cash wages of $1,000 or more to household employees, in the current or the prior year, and registers on Taxline State with its federal EIN (IRS Form SS-4). A liable employer stays liable for the rest of that year and the next.

Covered wages are cash wages paid to household employees: workers whose work the household controls, what is done and how. Not covered and not reported: wages paid to the employer's spouse, the employer's child under 21 or the employer's parent; workers supplied by an agency that controls their work (the agency is their employer and reports them); and self-employed contractors who control their own work.

2026: tax is due on the first $16,000 of covered wages paid to each employee in the calendar year (the wage base). The rate for a household employer in its first years is 3.4%; your account shows your rate.

Each quarter, report each covered employee's wages paid in the quarter, the total covered wages, the taxable wages (the part of each employee's wages that, with that employee's earlier covered wages this year, does not pass $16,000) and the tax (taxable wages times your rate, to the cent). Wages count in the quarter they are paid, not the quarter the work was done. The report and the tax are due by the 30th day of the month after the quarter ends, or the next business day when that is a weekend: third quarter 2026 by Friday 30 October 2026; fourth quarter by Monday 1 February 2027. A quarter's report opens the day after the quarter ends.

Report each new household employee whose wages are covered within 20 days of the first day of work for pay: name, Social Security number and that date. Do not report a worker whose wages are not covered (see covered). Do not report an employee already reported, unless they left and were rehired. The employees you have reported are on your account.
A wage report filed late: $75. Tax paid late: 10% of the tax unpaid, at least $25, and interest of 1% a month. A new-hire report filed late: $25 for each employee.
Filing and paying on Taxline State are free. Ostmere does not charge for, endorse or share data with any filing service.
